title: System Technologies Inc. v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Comprehensive Legal and Economic Analysis of System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 12211-21) and the Funded Research Exception
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: System Technologies v. Commissioner (Tax Court Docket No. 12211-21) addresses whether custom engineering projects paid through progress payments are excluded "funded research" under the federal R&D tax credit, IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). For U.S. manufacturers selling goods under Indiana law, Judge Buch denied the IRS's partial summary judgment motion, holding UCC refund remedies made payment contingent on research success.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The United States Tax Court litigation in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Docket No. 12211-21, represents a notable development (although, as a Tax Court order rather than a reported opinion, it is not binding precedent) in federal research and development (R&D) tax credit jurisprudence under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Presided over by Judge Ronald L. Buch, the proceedings center on the Commissioner's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, filed on August 1, 2024 (and frequently indexed in federal tax litigation databases alongside 2024 developments), which was resolved by the Tax Court's pivotal Order served on January 3, 2025, and followed, according to secondary reporting, by subsequent procedural orders in early 2025 addressing the Commissioner's motions to compel discovery responses (matters not addressed in the January 3, 2025 Order itself). The central legal controversy in the summary judgment phase was whether custom engineering and manufacturing projects executed under commercial purchase agreements requiring progress payments constituted excluded "funded research" within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4A(d)(1).
Taxpayer Profile and Claim History

System Technologies, Inc. is a corporation headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana, specializing in the custom engineering, design, and manufacture of complex industrial finishing systems primarily for the automotive manufacturing sector. The Court described the company's expertise as automotive coating designs and applications, such as pre-treatment solutions, ultraviolet (UV) curing systems, automatic liquid or powder systems, and robotic paint application systems.

System Technologies filed amended federal income tax returns for the tax years 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018 to claim research credits under IRC § 41. Specifically, for the 2016 tax year, the taxpayer claimed $99,304 in research credits based on development expenditures incurred across six custom finishing system projects. Of the 2016 credit amount, System Technologies utilized $46,307 to offset its 2016 income tax liability, carried back a portion to the 2015 tax year, and carried forward the remaining balance to the 2017 and 2018 tax years. On March 25, 2021, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued a Notice of Deficiency disallowing the claimed research credits in full across all four tax years. System Technologies filed a petition in the United States Tax Court challenging the Commissioner's determinations. Because the corporation's principal place of business is located in Indiana, appellate venue for the litigation lies with the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit pursuant to IRC § 7482(b)(1)(B).
The Six Disputed Business Components

The 2016 research credit claim was anchored in six bespoke industrial machinery projects, each initiated through a formal engineering and commercial proposal issued by System Technologies that incorporated standard terms and conditions, an exclusive limited warranty clause, and an express choice-of-law provision designating the laws of the State of Indiana as controlling.

body.text: The purchase agreements for these systems generally required the customers to remit progress payments to System Technologies while the engineering and manufacturing phases were actively underway. Furthermore, each proposal contained a uniform warranty provision warranting that the delivered equipment would be free from defects in material and workmanship under normal use and service, while explicitly stipulating that the customer's exclusive remedy for breach of warranty was limited to the repair or replacement of defective parts free of charge. Crucially, the warranty provision was silent regarding what remedy would apply if System Technologies failed in its engineering efforts and proved unable to deliver a completed, functioning system altogether.
Governing Statutory Framework and the IRS Challenge

To establish entitlement to the research credit under IRC § 41(a), a taxpayer must demonstrate that its expenditures qualify as "qualified research expenses" (QREs) incurred in carrying on a trade or business. Under IRC § 41(d)(1), activities constitute "qualified research" only if they satisfy a stringent four-part statutory test applied separately to each "business component," which IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) defines as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. First, under the Section 174 test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), the expenditures must be eligible to be treated as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 (the term "specified research or experimental expenditures" applies only to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, not to the 2016 tax year at issue), meaning the costs must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product. Second, under the technological information test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, relying fundamentally on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the business component test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) (as the Court labeled it), read together with the permitted purpose rules of § 41(d)(3)(A), the application of that technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, specifically relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Fourth, under the process of experimentation test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), substantially all—defined quantitatively by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more—of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose.

Even when a project satisfies all four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1), it is statutorily disqualified if it falls within one of the categorical exclusions enumerated in IRC § 41(d)(4). Among the most heavily litigated of these exclusions is IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes any research to the extent that it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. Because the statute itself does not define the term "funded," the substantive legal standard is governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), which is incorporated by cross-reference via Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9). To determine whether research performed pursuant to a customer contract is funded, the regulation mandates a two-prong inquiry under which all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons are considered. Under the financial risk or contingency prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research are not treated as funding. Conversely, if the researcher is entitled to retain payments regardless of whether the research succeeds, the customer bears the financial risk of failure, and the research is treated as funded. Under the substantial rights prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (3), even if payment is contingent on success, research is nevertheless treated as fully funded if the taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the research results under the terms of the agreement.

In its August 1, 2024 Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, the Commissioner sought a ruling as a matter of law that System Technologies' six 2016 projects were disqualified as funded research under the financial risk prong of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). The IRS argued that System Technologies bore no financial risk because the contracts mandated progress payments throughout project performance, contained no explicit refund or repayment requirement in the event of research failure, restricted the buyer's exclusive warranty remedy to the repair or replacement of defective parts free of charge, and involved commercial machinery where complete failure to deliver was not a realistic outcome contemplated by the contracting parties.
The Tax Court's Final Holding on Summary Judgment

Following supplemental briefing ordered by the Court regarding the application of the Indiana Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), Judge Buch denied the Commissioner's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment in the Order served January 3, 2025. Operating under Tax Court Rule 121(b), which permits summary judgment only when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and requires all factual inferences to be drawn in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party (Florida Peach Corp. v. Commissioner, 90 T.C. 678 (1988); Sundstrand Corp. v. Commissioner, 98 T.C. 518 (1992)), the Court held that System Technologies' research was not funded within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).

The Court's holding established a critical doctrinal link between federal tax regulations and state commercial law. Because every contract incorporated an Indiana choice-of-law provision and involved the sale of manufactured goods, the agreements were governed by Article 2 of the Indiana UCC. Under Indiana Code § 26-1-2-711(1), where a seller fails to make delivery, the buyer may cancel the contract and is statutorily entitled to recover so much of the price as has been paid. Addressing the IRS's contention that the exclusive "repair or replacement" warranty barred a refund, the Court invoked Indiana Code § 26-1-2-719(2) and Indiana precedent, together with federal district court authority applying Indiana law, including Kenworth of Indianapolis, Inc. v. Seventy-Seven Ltd., 134 N.E.3d 370 (Ind. 2019), Perry v. Gulf Stream Coach, Inc., 814 N.E.2d 634 (Ind. Ct. App. 2004), and Martin v. Thor Motor Coach Inc., 602 F. Supp. 3d 1087 (N.D. Ind. 2022). Under this body of commercial authority, an exclusive repair-or-replace remedy does not displace statutory UCC remedies in the event of a total breach; if System Technologies fails in its research and cannot deliver the promised product, repairing or replacing a component part is inadequate and fails of its essential purpose, thereby restoring the buyer's statutory right to a full refund of all progress payments. Consequently, ultimate payment to System Technologies was contingent on the success of its research, defeating the IRS's funded research challenge on summary judgment while leaving the remaining substantive and quantitative requirements of IRC § 41 for resolution through subsequent pretrial discovery, stipulation enforcement, and trial proceedings.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While System Technologies achieved a major procedural victory in defeating the Commissioner's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the funded research exclusion, a rigorous legal and technical post-mortem of Docket No. 12211-21 reveals severe contractual, evidentiary, and procedural deficiencies. Although the Order does not state the grounds on which the IRS disallowed the credits in full at examination, these vulnerabilities help explain why the funded research issue reached summary judgment, why the litigation escalated into protracted summary judgment and discovery battles, and why contractors relying on standard commercial documentation face existential disallowance risks in the United States Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit.
Contractual Silence and the Exclusive Warranty Trap

The primary catalyst for the dispute in System Technologies was a fundamental disconnect between standard commercial sales drafting and the regulatory demands of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). In federal R&D tax credit examinations, the IRS evaluates financial risk by scrutinizing the "four corners" of the executed agreements, looking for explicit language popularized in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), where the contract contained over 1,000 pages of technical specifications, a clause accepting total responsibility, and inspection and rejection terms, so that the contractor had no right to payment until it succeeded in each phase and payment remained at risk until the research was successfully completed and accepted. Conversely, in cases such as Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), federal appellate courts held that contracts lacking Fairchild-level specificity regarding success-based payment contingencies and explicit refund mechanics are treated as funded research.

System Technologies committed a classic contractual drafting failure by utilizing commercial proposals that demanded ongoing progress payments tied to project execution without explicitly stating in the contract text that those advances were refundable if the system failed performance acceptance testing. Compounding this omission, the proposals omitted any explicit contractual clause addressing the consequences of failed engineering, unsuccessful research, or total non-delivery of the custom finishing line, while simultaneously including a restrictive warranty clause stating that the customer's exclusive remedy for defects in materials or workmanship was the repair or replacement of defective parts free of charge. From the perspective of IRS examiners and Chief Counsel trial attorneys, this contractual architecture appeared fatal, because a vendor that collects progress payments during manufacturing and contractually limits the buyer's sole remedy to repairing or replacing defective parts appears legally insulated from having to refund the purchase price if the research fails. The Commissioner pursued the funded research issue through a formal Tax Court summary judgment proceeding—including court-ordered supplemental briefing on state commercial statutes—because System Technologies' commercial templates contained no express provision conditioning payment on successful completion of the research (and System Technologies did not identify one in its response).

Furthermore, relying on the Tax Court's UCC "gap-filler" rescue in System Technologies as a general tax planning strategy is perilous for two structural reasons. First, Ind. Code § 26-1-2-711 and § 26-1-2-719 apply exclusively to transactions in "goods" governed by UCC Article 2. When a taxpayer provides custom engineering, architectural design, or software development services governed by state common law rather than the UCC, statutory refund remedies for failure of an exclusive remedy's essential purpose do not automatically attach. Second, the Tax Court's subsequent merits decision in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50 (filed June 16, 2026, following earlier orders in that consolidated docket, including an Order served March 7, 2025), explicitly distinguished System Technologies. In Smith, the Tax Court refused to extend the local-law rationale of System Technologies to architectural service contracts governed by the laws of Dubai and England (reasoning that those contracts themselves provided an adequate remedy, unlike the contracts in System Technologies, and that foreign-law provisions not expressly incorporated into the agreements could not override their terms), holding that milestone payments under all six sample projects were not contingent on research success and that the taxpayer lost the credits entirely on projects where it failed to retain substantial intellectual property rights. Thus, contractual silence regarding research failure remains a severe vulnerability that only fortuitous UCC Article 2 applicability and an explicit Indiana choice-of-law clause salvaged in System Technologies.
Fragmented Contract Chains and Multi-Document Integration Vulnerabilities

A second potential vulnerability, visible in the undisputed contractual background recited in Judge Buch's Order (which, as a summary judgment ruling, made no findings of fact and did not characterize the documentation as deficient), was the fragmented, multi-year documentation chain governing the six projects. Rather than executing a single, integrated Master Research and Manufacturing Agreement prior to the commencement of work—as contemplated by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), which requires that all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons be considered in determining funding—System Technologies operated through disjointed commercial exchanges. In Project 352 (the Mercury project) and Project 354 (the Tomita project), the initial proposals were issued in 2015, followed by subsequent sales orders, a Tomita purchase order, a Mercury supplemental proposal, and a Mercury drop-ship order (the Order dates only the Mercury sales order, to 2016). Similarly, in Project 356 (the Wilhelm project), a 2016 commercial proposal was subsequently followed by a subcontractor agreement between System Technologies and Wilhelm for the same products, and in Project 359 (the Orlick project), a 2016 proposal and purchase requisition were followed by 2017 upgrade orders.

This fragmented "battle of the forms" presented a latent risk, although the Order records that neither party disputed the terms of the contracts at issue, only their legal meaning. In commercial equipment manufacturing, customer-issued purchase orders and general contractor subcontract agreements routinely contain integration ("entire agreement") clauses and conflicting choice-of-law or intellectual property forfeiture provisions that supersede the vendor's initial proposal. Under Seventh Circuit contract modification principles (Large v. Mobile Tool Int'l, Inc., 724 F.3d 766 (7th Cir. 2013); Curia v. Nelson, 587 F.3d 824 (7th Cir. 2009)), a subsequent agreement modifies an original contract to the extent its terms are inconsistent. For Projects 352, 356, and 359, the Order recites that the subsequent supplemental proposal, drop-ship order, subcontractor agreement, and upgrade agreement incorporated, related back to, or did not modify the original 2015 and 2016 proposal terms, and the Court found that all purchase orders contained or incorporated by reference the Indiana choice-of-law provisions. Had Wilhelm Construction Company's subcontractor agreement contained a standard superseding integration clause stripping out System Technologies' proposal terms or substituting an unfavorable jurisdiction's law, or had customer purchase orders forfeited substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), those specific projects could have faced a materially stronger funded research challenge (an issue the Court had no occasion to decide).
Conflation of Economic Risk and Section 174 Technical Uncertainty

The litigation record in System Technologies also highlights a critical analytical collision between the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and the threshold technical uncertainty requirement of IRC § 174. In seeking summary judgment, the Commissioner argued that a complete failure by System Technologies to deliver the bargained-for finishing equipment was not a "realistic outcome" because the parties never drafted contract clauses anticipating total non-delivery.

While Judge Buch properly rejected this argument on summary judgment—pointing out that factual inferences must favor the non-moving taxpayer under Tax Court Rule 121 and that questions regarding the certainty of product delivery pertain to IRC § 174 eligibility rather than IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funding—the IRS's argument, which the Court observed may raise a fact question under the section 174 test, signals a potential evidentiary vulnerability in the taxpayer's contemporaneous technical records. Specifically, System Technologies' commercial proposals are not characterized in the Order beyond their warranty and choice-of-law terms, but because the Commissioner expressly argued that neither System Technologies nor its customers doubted delivery, the IRS may portray them at trial as routine production and fabrication quotes for established categories of industrial equipment (spray washers, blow-off stages, hydroflush cells, and powder booths) rather than engineering development contracts confronting genuine technological uncertainty. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty exists only if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product. When a custom machinery manufacturer issues a fixed-price proposal warranting solely against defects in material and workmanship without documenting the specific fluid-dynamic, thermal, chemical, or mechanical design uncertainties inside the proposal or an attached engineering specification matrix, it invites the IRS to contend at trial that the project was merely routine custom fabrication and adaptation of existing commercial designs (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and (C)) where successful delivery was never in doubt.
Post-Summary Judgment Discovery, Stipulation, and Substantiation Failures

Crucially, the Tax Court's January 3, 2025 denial of partial summary judgment on the funded research issue did not validate System Technologies' research credits or resolve the deficiency. Instead, it merely defeated the Commissioner's summary judgment challenge under a single threshold exclusion, shifting the battleground directly into rigorous pretrial discovery and evidentiary substantiation of the four-part test and QRE calculations. Following the summary judgment order, Docket No. 12211-21 immediately bogged down in contentious procedural disputes over evidentiary adequacy. As reported in secondary sources (these post-summary-judgment proceedings are not addressed in the January 3, 2025 Order), the docket involved two Motions to Compel Responses to Interrogatories filed by the Commissioner on January 24 and January 31, 2025, which the Court reportedly granted on February 21, 2025, highlighting the unforgiving nature of Tax Court discovery when a taxpayer struggles to produce granular, project-by-project technical and financial substantiation linking specific employee activities to the statutory elements of IRC § 41(d). Furthermore, the January 31, 2025 filing, as reported, was the Commissioner's second Motion to Compel, which targeted System Technologies' answers on wage allocation, fabrication-team experimentation, and the technical details of the ten Gosiger machines, rather than a Rule 91(f) motion by System Technologies. In resolving these motions, Judge Buch reportedly found the responses incomplete and directed supplementation by March 14, 2025; separately, although the stipulation process under Rule 91(a)(1) is often described as the "bedrock of Tax Court practice," the Court will compel stipulation only where the parties agree or where facts are uncontroverted, refusing to force a party to stipulate to disputed evidentiary characterizations or unverified retrofitted summaries regarding research qualification.

These procedural clashes reflect the formidable substantive burden awaiting System Technologies at trial under controlling Seventh Circuit precedent in Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023). Because System Technologies' case is appealable to the Seventh Circuit, the Tax Court is bound under the Golsen rule (Golsen v. Commissioner, 54 T.C. 742 (1970)) to apply the Seventh Circuit's strict interpretation of the "substantially all" test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)) and the "shrinking-back" rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)). In Little Sandy Coal—as well as subsequent Tax Court decisions such as Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (filed December 23, 2024)—courts have established three fatal evidentiary pitfalls that directly threaten custom equipment manufacturers like System Technologies.

First, taxpayers frequently fall victim to the "all-or-nothing" whole-system fallacy. Defining the business component as an entire industrial finishing line or spray washer system (such as Project 352's entire Powder Finishing System or Project 355's three-stage inline washer) requires proving that at least 80% of all research activities performed on that entire machine constituted elements of a process of experimentation. In custom manufacturing, assembling structural frames, standard conveyor drives, plumbing, and routine electrical panels involves known engineering methods, and as the Seventh Circuit held in Little Sandy Coal, the novelty of a custom-built machine is not, by itself, a substitute for showing that substantially all research activities were elements of a process of experimentation. Second, taxpayers forfeit the protection of the shrinking-back rule when they lack subcomponent cost accounting. When an overall machine fails the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) allows the taxpayer to shrink back the analysis to the most significant subset of elements (such as a novel high-velocity blow-off nozzle manifold in Project 354 or a specific high-pressure hydroflush cell geometry in Project 357). However, if the taxpayer tracked labor hours and supply costs only at the top-level project number without subcomponent time-tracking codes, the court lacks a principled evidentiary basis to shrink back, resulting in a total disallowance of the project's QREs. Third, the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal clarified that while direct supervision and direct support of research (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)) can be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 80% substantially all fraction, taxpayers cannot rely on generalized descriptions of uncertainty or arbitrary, non-contemporaneous percentage estimates of employee time; evidentiary records must concretely connect specific employee activities, iterative hypothesis testing, and pilot-model work to the experimental process.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, commercial law, and procedural requirement implicated in System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 12211-21) and its controlling Seventh Circuit judicial framework against the specific taxpayer vulnerabilities, IRS challenges, and the Court's governing standard of proof.

The Court's Standard of Proof & Legal Holding

cells: Funded Research Exclusion: Financial Risk & Payment Contingency
IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995).

System Technologies' proposals required customer progress payments during manufacturing and omitted explicit contract language requiring repayment or refunds if the research failed or the system was not delivered. The IRS moved for partial summary judgment, asserting that payments were non-contingent.

Standard: Payment must be contingent on the success of the research (paid for the product or result). Holding: Motion denied. The Court evaluates the entire agreement alongside governing state law. Because Indiana law mandates a refund of progress payments if the seller fails to deliver, ultimate payment is contingent on research success.
State Law Buyer Remedies for Non-Delivery
Ind. Code § 26-1-2-711(1) (Indiana Uniform Commercial Code - Sales).

The written contracts were completely silent regarding buyer remedies if System Technologies failed to deliver a functioning, completed industrial finishing system. The IRS argued that the absence of an express contractual refund clause meant the taxpayer retained payments regardless of success.

Standard: Where a contract incorporates a valid state choice-of-law clause and involves the sale of goods, statutory UCC remedies fill contractual gaps. Holding: Under Ind. Code § 26-1-2-711(1), if a seller fails to deliver due to failed research, the buyer may cancel and recover "so much of the price as has been paid," establishing economic risk under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1).
Contractual Limitation of Remedies & Failure of Essential Purpose
Ind. Code § 26-1-2-719(2); Kenworth of Indianapolis, Inc. v. Seventy-Seven Ltd., 134 N.E.3d 370 (Ind. 2019); Martin v. Thor Motor Coach Inc., 602 F. Supp. 3d 1087 (N.D. Ind. 2022).

Every proposal contained a warranty clause limiting the customer's exclusive remedy to the repair or replacement of defective parts free of charge. The IRS contended that this exclusive remedy legally precluded the customer from demanding a cash refund for failed research.

Standard: Under Ind. Code § 26-1-2-719(2), where circumstances cause an exclusive or limited remedy to "fail of its essential purpose," general UCC remedies apply. Holding: Exclusive repair or replacement remedies do not bar state remedies in cases of total breach. If research fails and the product cannot be delivered, repairing a part fails of its essential purpose, triggering the statutory right to a full refund.
Multi-Document Contractual Chain Integration
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); State Contract Modification Principles (Large v. Mobile Tool Int'l, Inc., 724 F.3d 766 (7th Cir. 2013)).

Projects 352, 354, 355, 356, 357, and 359 involved fragmented document chains (2015 proposals for Projects 352 and 354 and 2016 proposals for the rest, followed by sales orders (Mercury's dated 2016), customer purchase orders, a Mercury supplemental proposal and drop-ship order, a subcontractor agreement with Wilhelm Construction, and 2017 upgrades for Orlick). Risk existed that later documents superseded the original choice-of-law or risk terms.

Standard: Funding status is determined by examining all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and other persons; a subsequent agreement modifies an original contract only to the extent inconsistent. Holding: Because all purchase orders contained or incorporated by reference Indiana choice-of-law provisions, and the subsequent documents for Projects 352, 356, and 359 incorporated, related back to, or did not modify the original proposals' Indiana choice-of-law provisions, the UCC refund obligation remained intact across all six projects.
Substantial Rights Retention in Research Results
IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50.

Even where payment is contingent on success, research is funded if the contractor forfeits substantial rights to use the research results in its business without paying the customer. Standard customer purchase orders often contain boilerplate IP assignment clauses.

Standard: The taxpayer must retain the right to use the research results in its trade or business without paying for that right; retaining mere general engineering experience or skill is insufficient. Holding: While not the basis of the IRS's August 2024 motion in System Technologies, the Court in Smith confirmed that both contingency and substantial rights must be satisfied by reference to the terms of the research agreements, declining to apply foreign-law provisions not expressly incorporated into those agreements.
Section 174 Technical Uncertainty vs. Remote Risk of Failure
IRC §§ 41(d)(1)(A) & 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1); Tax Court Rule 121(b).

The IRS argued that total non-delivery of the industrial washers and coating systems was not a "realistic outcome" expected by the parties, pointing to the routine commercial framing of the proposals.

Standard: On summary judgment (Rule 121), factual inferences are drawn in favor of the non-movant. Substantively, whether successful delivery is uncertain is an inquiry under IRC § 174 (capability, method, or appropriate design uncertainty), not an element of the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funding test. Holding: The IRS's "remote risk" argument failed on summary judgment, but the taxpayer retains the burden of proving actual IRC § 174 technical uncertainty at trial.
Process of Experimentation, "Substantially All" (80%), & Shrinking-Back
IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. §§ 1.41-4(a)(6) & 1.41-4(b)(2); Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023); Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113.

Claiming whole industrial finishing lines as single business components risks failing the 80% activity threshold due to non-experimental fabrication, assembly, and routine testing. Without subcomponent time and cost tracking, the taxpayer cannot shrink back to qualifying subsystems.

Standard: At least 80% of a business component's research activities (measured by activities, including direct supervision and support in numerator and denominator) must constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation evaluating alternatives. Novelty and arbitrary estimates fail. Holding: Denial of summary judgment on funding does not establish credit eligibility; the taxpayer must prove the 80% test at the whole-system or properly substantiated subcomponent level.
Pretrial Discovery & Stipulation Enforcement
IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); Tax Court Rules 70, 71, 91(a)(1), and 91(f).

Contentious pretrial clashes over the IRS's Motions to Compel Responses to Interrogatories (filed Jan. 24 and Jan. 31, 2025, and reportedly granted Feb. 21, 2025), which challenged generalized, non-component-specific answers on the process of experimentation, wage allocation, and the Gosiger machines.

Standard: Notices of Deficiency carry a presumption of correctness; tax credits are a matter of legislative grace (INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79 (1992)). Under Rules 70, 71, and 104, interrogatory answers must be complete and specific to each business component; generalized narratives, photographs, specification sheets, and retroactive percentage allocations were reportedly held insufficient. Rule 91(f) relief is likewise limited to matters not genuinely in dispute.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal holdings and evidentiary warnings of System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner and its controlling Seventh Circuit companion authority, Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, into actionable tax and legal practice, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate how United States taxpayers must restructure their commercial and engineering operations. Each case study models a realistic commercial scenario confronting the exact pitfalls identified in Docket No. 12211-21 and details a sequential four-pillar remediation framework covering project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Custom Thermal-Chemical Surface Treatment Equipment Manufacturer (UCC Article 2 Goods with Progress Billing and Subcontractor Overlays)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Vanguard Surface Engineering Corp. ("Vanguard"), an Indiana-based manufacturer of custom industrial aqueous pre-treatment tunnels and robotic powder-coating booths for Tier-1 automotive suppliers, plans to claim IRC § 41 research credits for its 2026 development of a multi-stage, zero-discharge chemical conversion wash system ("Project 410") ordered by a prime construction contractor, Apex Industrial Builders ("Apex"), for installation at an electric vehicle battery enclosure plant. Under Vanguard's legacy commercial workflow—which mirrors the multi-document contractual structure of Project 352 (Mercury) and Project 356 (Wilhelm) in System Technologies—Vanguard issues a 2025 budgetary quote requiring a 30% deposit upon order, 40% upon delivery of steel housing modules, and 30% upon shipment. Vanguard's boilerplate quote includes a warranty limiting the buyer's exclusive remedy to the "repair or replacement of defective mechanical parts for 12 months" and remains entirely silent regarding failed research or system-level performance acceptance. Six months later, Apex issues a standard construction Subcontractor Agreement containing a general integration clause, a choice-of-law provision designating a jurisdiction that strictly enforces commercial remedy limitations, and a "Work Made for Hire" clause granting Apex exclusive ownership of all custom engineering drawings and programmable logic controller (PLC) software code. Meanwhile, Vanguard's engineers charge all labor to a single top-level job code ("Job 410"), blending novel computational fluid dynamics (CFD) nozzle design with routine sheet-metal welding and field installation.

If audited by the IRS, Vanguard faces catastrophic disallowance across four fronts. First, Apex's Subcontractor Agreement legally supersedes Vanguard's initial proposal under standard contract modification rules. Second, the exclusive repair-or-replace warranty coupled with progress payments triggers a funded research disallowance under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) if the governing state law does not apply the UCC failure-of-essential-purpose doctrine as liberally as Indiana. Third, the intellectual property assignment strips Vanguard of substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Fourth, the single job code prevents Vanguard from satisfying the 80% substantially all test at the whole-machine level or shrinking back to qualifying subsystems under Little Sandy Coal.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance Restructuring

Vanguard must establish a formal Stage-Gate R&D and Commercial Governance Protocol prior to executing any customer order or commencing engineering work, thereby aligning every agreement that will be considered under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). At Gate 0 (Pre-Bid Technical and Tax Decomposition), before issuing the commercial proposal to Apex, Vanguard's Chief Engineer and Tax Director must decompose Project 410 into a hierarchy of discrete business components and subcomponents pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Rather than treating the entire 120-foot wash tunnel as a single business component, Gate 0 governance isolates two specific high-risk subcomponents where genuine capability and design uncertainty exist—specifically, Subcomponent 410-A (the High-Velocity Ultrasonic Air-Knife Blow-Off Manifold) and Subcomponent 410-B (the Closed-Loop Zirconium Counter-Flow Filtration Module)—while explicitly segregating Subcomponent 410-C (the structural stainless-steel housing, standard plumbing, and conveyor drive) as non-qualifying routine commercial production. At Gate 1 (Contractual Alignment Review), corporate legal counsel must review all subsequent purchase orders, supplemental proposals, drop-ship orders, and general contractor subcontract agreements before execution to prevent unintentional contract modifications from stripping choice-of-law, acceptance testing, or risk-allocation terms.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Restructuring

To neutralize the IRS's argument in System Technologies that non-delivery or technical failure was not a realistic outcome and to establish threshold eligibility under IRC § 174, Vanguard must replace generic commercial sales descriptions with a contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty and Design Specification Matrix (TUDSM) attached directly as Schedule A to the commercial proposal. Schedule A must document that existing commercial air-knife blow-off systems cannot evaporate trapped aqueous chemical films from deep-draw EV battery housings within a 14-second line tact time without causing thermal warping exceeding , and must explicitly state that the appropriate manifold geometry, nozzle impingement angle, and acoustic frequency required to achieve complete moisture removal without thermal distortion are uncertain at the outset of the project. Throughout development, engineers must record each design iteration inside a centralized Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) log, detailing the specific scientific hypothesis tested in each CFD simulation run, the empirical test data generated during physical pilot-cell trials, and the exact technical parameters that failed before arriving at the final validated geometry.
Step 3: Contract Terms Restructuring

Rather than relying exclusively on post-hoc state UCC litigation to prove that a limited warranty fails of its essential purpose under Ind. Code § 26-1-2-719(2), Vanguard must embed explicit Fairchild-grade risk allocation, UCC preservation, and IP retention clauses directly into its Master Proposal Terms and Conditions, and execute a binding overriding addendum to Apex's Subcontractor Agreement. First, Vanguard must insert an Express Order of Precedence and Relation-Back Clause stipulating that any subsequent sales order, purchase order, subcontractor agreement, or upgrade requisition issued in connection with Project 410 relates back to and is governed strictly by the risk allocation, acceptance, choice-of-law, and intellectual property provisions of the original proposal, and that no integration clause in a subsequent purchase order or subcontract shall supersede or modify those terms unless explicitly referencing that section in a writing signed by corporate officers of both parties. Second, Vanguard must include an Explicit Performance Acceptance and Refundable Financing Advances Clause stating that all milestone or progress payments remitted by the buyer prior to Final Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) constitute conditional financing advances, that ultimate payment is strictly contingent upon Vanguard's successful engineering, delivery, and commissioning of a system meeting the quantitative technical performance metrics in Schedule A, and that if Vanguard fails to achieve Schedule A performance specifications or fails to deliver a functioning system, the buyer may reject the equipment, cancel the agreement, and receive a full refund of all progress payments previously paid. Third, Vanguard must draft a Bifurcated Warranty and UCC Remedy Preservation Clause clarifying that the limited warranty restricting remedies to the repair or replacement of defective materials or workmanship applies solely after successful completion of SAT and formal written acceptance of the functioning system by the buyer, whereas prior to formal acceptance—or in the event Vanguard fails in its research and engineering to deliver a system capable of achieving Schedule A specifications—the repair-or-replacement limitation shall not apply, and the buyer retains all statutory remedies under Indiana Code § 26-1-2-711(1), including full recovery of all price payments remitted. Fourth, Vanguard must incorporate a Substantial Rights Retention Clause providing that, notwithstanding any "Work Made for Hire" language in any subcontract, Vanguard retains full, non-exclusive, perpetual ownership and substantial rights in all underlying engineering methodologies, fluid-dynamic designs, nozzle geometries, discoveries, and software algorithms developed during Project 410, with the unrestricted right to utilize such research results in manufacturing systems for other commercial customers without payment of royalties or fees to the buyer.
Step 4: Experimentation & QRE Tracking Restructuring

To survive a Seventh Circuit Little Sandy Coal examination and prevent Tax Court Rule 71 and Rule 91(f) discovery and stipulation disputes, Vanguard must overhaul its Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and timekeeping architecture. Vanguard must abolish top-level job costing ("Job 410") and mandate that employees log time daily against granular Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) codes tied directly to the Gate 0 subcomponents: 410-A.1 for Blow-Off Manifold CFD Modeling and Hypothesis Testing, 410-A.2 for Manifold Prototype Fabrication and Direct Support, 410-A.3 for Empirical Air-Velocity Trial Testing, 410-B.1 for Filtration Module Experimentation, and 410-C.0 for Non-Qualifying Structural Frame Assembly and Routine Quality Control. For each qualifying subcomponent (410-A and 410-B), the tax department must verify the exact Little Sandy Coal activity ratio quarterly:

By isolating routine structural assembly into 410-C.0 (which is excluded from the credit claim altogether) and contemporaneously documenting the direct nexus between prototype technicians' support hours (410-A.2) and the experimental testing (410-A.3), Vanguard ensures that Subcomponents 410-A and 410-B independently exceed the 80% threshold, creating an unassailable, audit-ready record suitable for immediate stipulation under Tax Court Rule 91(a)(1).
Case Study 2: Bespoke Automated Robotics & Machine-Vision Integration Firm (Hybrid Engineering Services and Hardware Under Multi-Jurisdictional Contracts)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Aether Automation & Vision, Inc. ("Aether"), a Chicago, Illinois engineering and systems integration firm whose tax disputes are appealable to the Seventh Circuit, designs custom six-axis robotic laser-ablation and machine-vision inspection cells for aerospace and defense manufacturers. In 2026, Aether enters into three Master Services Agreements (MSAs) to develop a high-speed automated composite micro-fracture ablation cell ("Project 700"). Unlike pure equipment sales, Aether's contracts are drafted as "Engineering Design and Integration Services Agreements" billed on a monthly milestone schedule based on engineering hours expended and design review completions. One customer is a European aerospace conglomerate whose MSA designates the law of a foreign jurisdiction, while the other two MSAs designate Illinois law but classify the engagement as professional engineering services rather than a sale of goods. The contracts require Aether to correct engineering errors at its own expense for 90 days post-delivery, but contain no clause requiring Aether to refund milestone payments if the machine-vision laser algorithm fails to achieve the target sub-micron defect ablation rate. For tax purposes, Aether's Chief Financial Officer claims 65% of the Chief Operating Officer's (COO) salary and 80% of all engineering staff wages based on year-end executive interviews estimating how much time the team spent on innovative projects.

Under the legal framework established in System Technologies, Smith v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-50), and Little Sandy Coal, Aether's claim is fatally defective on three independent grounds. First, because Aether's contracts are structured as professional engineering services rather than sales of goods under UCC Article 2, Aether cannot rely on UCC § 2-711(1) or § 2-719(2) (as System Technologies did under Ind. Code §§ 26-1-2-711 and 26-1-2-719) to imply a statutory refund remedy upon failed research. Furthermore, regarding the foreign-law contract, the Tax Court in Smith explicitly declined to apply the System Technologies local-law rationale to rescue milestone service contracts governed by foreign or non-UCC legal frameworks. Second, because milestone payments are tied to engineering design reviews and hours worked rather than ultimate technical success, the payments are non-contingent under Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Smith. Third, relying on year-end executive interviews and arbitrary percentage allocations for the COO and engineering staff violates controlling Seventh Circuit precedent, including Little Sandy Coal and recent Seventh Circuit decisions affirming the disallowance of executive compensation where payroll records established compensation paid but failed to substantiate the specific time devoted to qualifying research services.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance Restructuring

Aether must transition from an ad-hoc consulting governance model to a structured Turnkey Deliverable and Experimental Governance Framework. Corporate governance policies must prohibit sales executives from executing time-and-materials or hours-based milestone service agreements for R&D-eligible projects, mandating instead that every developmental project be governed by a Turnkey System Delivery Policy under which Aether assumes full financial responsibility for delivering a validated hardware-software business component. Simultaneously, to include any portion of the COO's or Vice President of Engineering's compensation under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) as direct supervision of qualified research, corporate governance protocols must strictly separate general management, administrative oversight, and commercial status meetings—which are statutorily excluded indirect activities—from first-line technical supervision of specific experimental hypotheses.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Restructuring

Aether must institute a mandatory Scientific Method and Iterative Experimentation Dossier (SMIED) for Project 700 that directly satisfies the Seventh Circuit's scientific-method standard articulated in Little Sandy Coal. Before writing a single line of machine-vision code or assembling optical hardware, the lead engineer must document the baseline technical uncertainty in the SMIED, specifying that existing technical knowledge does not establish whether a 532 nm picosecond laser coupled with a coaxial hyperspectral camera can ablate carbon-fiber surface contaminants without inducing subsurface thermal delamination in aerospace panels moving at 2.5 meters per second. The SMIED must contemporaneously log each distinct technical alternative evaluated—such as comparing galvanometric mirror scanning with thermal infrared feedback against polygon scanning with coaxial optical coherence tomography and multi-beam diffractive optics with real-time neural-network pulse modulation—recording the mathematical modeling, benchtop pilot-model trials, failure modes, and quantitative empirical data generated across each iteration. Furthermore, all engineering test logs must explicitly segregate experimental validation testing conducted to resolve design uncertainty during development (which qualifies under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C)) from post-development production quality control, routine calibration, or ordinary inspection (which are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)).
Step 3: Contract Terms Restructuring

To eliminate the fatal legal distinction between non-contingent service contracts (Smith, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson) and UCC goods contracts (System Technologies), Aether must restructure its MSAs and Statements of Work (SOWs) as predominant turnkey equipment and software delivery contracts governed explicitly by domestic UCC law and unequivocal contractual refund obligations. First, Aether must incorporate an Express Domestic Choice of Law and UCC Opt-In Clause providing that the agreement and all associated SOWs shall be construed under and governed by the internal laws of the State of Illinois or the State of Indiana without regard to conflict-of-law principles, and that the parties expressly agree that the predominant purpose of the contract is the design, manufacture, and delivery of a turnkey automated physical system (a "good") governed in its entirety by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code as enacted in the governing state, including all statutory buyer remedies for non-delivery or rejection under UCC § 2-711. Second, Aether must replace all hours-based or calendar-based billing milestones with a Strict Technical Acceptance Contingency and Clawback Clause stipulating that no payment under the agreement is earned based on engineering hours expended, that all interim progress remittances are provisional advances subject to full repayment, and that if Aether fails to demonstrate during Final Acceptance Testing that the Project 700 cell achieves a 99.98% micro-fracture detection and ablation accuracy at 2.5 meters per second with zero subsurface delamination, the buyer may reject the system and terminate the contract for cause, whereupon Aether must refund 100% of all interim payments within 30 days and bear the entire financial cost of all unsuccessful research, labor, and prototype materials. Third, to avoid the partial disallowance suffered by the taxpayer in Smith v. Commissioner, Aether must include an Explicit Allocation of Substantial Rights Clause stating that the buyer receives title solely to the physical unit delivered upon final acceptance and a non-exclusive license to operate the embedded software on that unit, while Aether retains sole and substantial rights to all foreground research results, machine-vision training architectures, laser pulse-modulation techniques, and engineering know-how discovered during Project 700, with the unrestricted right to commercialize such innovations for third parties without fee or restriction.
Step 4: Experimentation & QRE Tracking Restructuring

To satisfy the substantiation mandates of IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), and Seventh Circuit case law, Aether must eliminate retrospective percentage estimates entirely. Aether must integrate its software repository (Git/Jira) and mechanical CAD vault with its payroll timekeeping system so that engineers record hours contemporaneously on a daily or bi-weekly basis against specific experimental tickets linked directly to the SMIED hypotheses, such as Ticket 700-OPT-04: Coaxial OCT Sensor Alignment Experimentation. With respect to executive compensation, Aether must prohibit claiming any generalized percentage of the COO's wages. When the COO performs qualifying direct supervision of research—such as reviewing failed laser delamination test data directly with the optical physicist and directing the next experimental pulse-width modification—the COO must log the exact hours spent on that specific technical session contemporaneously, corroborated by dated design-review minutes demonstrating the COO's direct technical direction. Finally, prior to filing any original or amended tax return, Aether must compile a comprehensive substantiation binder mapping each business component, the specific research activities performed for each component, the total qualified employee wage, supply, and contract research expenses, and the governing contract risk provisions. By maintaining this granular, contemporaneous nexus between state commercial law remedies, subcomponent technical uncertainty, and activity-based time records, the taxpayer constructs a rigorous evidentiary foundation capable of prevailing both on summary judgment and on the merits in the United States Tax Court.
